/-!
# Erdős Problem 1133

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1133](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1133)
- [Er67] Erdős, P., Problems and results on the convergence and divergence properties of the
  Lagrange interpolation polynomials and some extremal problems. Mathematica (Cluj) (1967), 65-73.
-/

open Filter Set

namespace Erdos1133

/--
Let $C>0$. There exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently large the following holds.

For any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ there exist $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in [-1,1]$ such that, if $P$ is a
polynomial of degree $m<(1+\epsilon)n$ with $P(x_i)=y_i$ for at least $(1-\epsilon)n$ many
$1\leq i\leq n$, then $$\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert >C.$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 26 41]
theorem erdos_1133 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ C > (0 : ℝ), ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      ∀ x : Fin n → Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1,
        ∃ y : Fin n → Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1,
          ∀ P : Polynomial ℝ,
            (P.natDegree : ℝ) < (1 + ε) * (n : ℝ) →
            ((Finset.univ.filter (fun i ↦ P.eval (x i : ℝ) = (y i : ℝ))).card : ℝ) ≥
              (1 - ε) * (n : ℝ) →
            ∃ z ∈ Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1, |P.eval z| > C := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős proved that, for any $C>0$, there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently
large and $m=\lfloor (1+\epsilon)n\rfloor$ then for any $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in [-1,1]$ there is a
polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ such that $\lvert P(x_i)\rvert\leq 1$ for $1\leq i\leq m$ and
$\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert>C$. The conjectured statement would also imply this, but
Erdős in [Er67] says he could not even prove it for $m=n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 26 41]
theorem erdos_1133.variants.weaker :
    ∀ C > (0 : ℝ), ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      let m := ⌊(1 + ε) * (n : ℝ)⌋₊;
      ∀ x : Fin m → Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1,
        ∃ P : Polynomial ℝ,
          P.natDegree = n ∧
          (∀ i : Fin m, |P.eval (x i : ℝ)| ≤ 1) ∧
          ∃ z ∈ Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1, |P.eval z| > C := by
  sorry

end Erdos1133

reformulations.difference: The source concludes that the maximum of |P| on [-1,1] exceeds C; Lean instead asserts the existence of a point where |P| exceeds C.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The absolute value of a real polynomial is continuous on the nonempty compact interval [-1,1], so it attains its maximum. Thus a value exceeds C exactly when the maximum exceeds C. The precise equivalence with C < sSup of the image was proved in the scratch file.

reformulations.difference: The source's maximum bound is expressed as an existential pointwise bound.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The same compactness and continuity argument applies to the polynomial supplied by this theorem. The pointwise bound is equivalent to the maximum bound; this local equivalence was proved in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The primary paper uses ordered distinct nodes, whereas Lean allows arbitrary indexed families, including repetitions. The website also uses arbitrary families.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Given the distinct-node statement with parameter η, choose 0 < δ ≤ min(η/4, 1/4). Let r be the number of distinct nodes among n inputs. If r < (1−δ)n, assign different labels to copies of each node; any polynomial then matches at most r indices. Otherwise apply the source statement to r representatives and extend their labels arbitrarily. At least (1−δ)n total matches give at least r−δn ≥ (1−η)r representative matches, while (1+δ)n < (1+η)r. Also r ≥ 3n/4, so the representative count is sufficiently large uniformly. Sorting only permutes indices. The reverse implication follows by restricting to distinct families. The numerical inequalities, but not the full combinatorial equivalence, were proved in Lean.

reformulations.difference: Lean permits repeated nodes, while Theorem 4 in the primary paper lists distinct ordered nodes.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Extend the distinct values in any repeated m-tuple to a set of m distinct points of [-1,1]. The polynomial provided for this enlarged set satisfies every original sample constraint, with unchanged degree and maximum bound. Conversely, the arbitrary-family statement applies to distinct families. Ordering is immaterial.
